nameStory: The Sharp-tailed Sandpiper gets its name from its most distinctive feature - the pointed, narrow tail feathers that come to a sharp point when folded. Unlike many of its sandpiper cousins with more rounded or square-cut tails, this bird's tail looks like it was carefully trimmed with scissors to create that signature sharp edge.
description: The Sharp-tailed Sandpiper is a medium-sized shorebird that's like finding a needle in a haystack along New England's coast. This Asian wanderer occasionally shows up during migration, standing about robin-sized among the mudflats and beaches. It has the typical sandpiper build with long legs for wading, a straight bill for probing mud, and mottled brown and buff plumage that helps it blend into sandy shores. With only 10 recorded sightings in New England, spotting one is a true birding treasure.

idTips.label: Pointed tail
idTips.description: The tail feathers form a sharp, narrow point when folded - you can see this distinctive triangular shape even when the bird is walking and feeding

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Straight, dark bill that's slightly thicker at the base and feels substantial when seen through binoculars - not needle-thin like some sandpipers

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Yellow-green to olive legs that look almost muddy in color, helping the bird blend with wet sand and marsh edges

idTips.label: Breast streaking
idTips.description: Fine, dark streaks across a buffy-white breast that create a subtle necklace pattern, more organized than the random spotting of some relatives

idTips.label: Size and posture
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than Least Sandpipers but smaller than Dunlin, with an upright, alert stance when not feeding

habitat: In New England, Sharp-tailed Sandpipers turn up on mudflats, salt marshes, and sandy beaches where other migrating shorebirds gather. Look for them along protected bays and estuaries where gentle waves deposit rich organic matter that attracts small invertebrates. They prefer areas with both wet mud for probing and drier sand for resting, often near patches of salt marsh grass.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare during spring migration (May), but any sightings would show birds in transitional plumage with fresh feather edges.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during summer as they breed in Siberian tundra thousands of miles away.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for sightings during fall migration (August-October) when juveniles with crisp, fresh plumage may appear among flocks of other sandpipers.
seasonality.winter: Not present in New England winters - these birds continue south to Australia and Southeast Asia for their winter homes.

funFact: Sharp-tailed Sandpipers make one of the longest migrations on Earth, flying roughly 15,000 miles from Siberian breeding grounds to Australian beaches - and the few that show up in New England are essentially lost on one of nature's most epic journeys!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Pectoral Sandpipers, which are much more common in New England. Remember 'Sharp tail, Pectoral pecs' - Sharp-tailed has that pointed tail while Pectoral Sandpiper has a sharply defined dark breast band that looks like pectoral muscles, plus a more rounded tail.
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily an Asian species that breeds in Siberia and winters in Australia, making any New England sighting a significant rarity. Most North American records are from Alaska and the West Coast, so finding one here represents a major navigational error during their transcontinental journey.
compareHints: Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band. It's larger than Least Sandpipers and has different leg color than the bright yellow-legged Least. The pointed tail and overall size help separate it from the smaller 'peeps' and larger species like Dunlin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
